investment_summary:
Nu Holdings grew 2025 revenue 37.0% to US$15.8 billion and net income 45.6% to US$2.87 billion [1]. Free cash flow reached US$3.16 billion, but gross margin fell to 42.0% from 45.6% as credit losses and deposit costs outgrew revenue [1].

Valuation is the central question. The reverse DCF implies only 4.0% annual revenue growth over ten years at the current enterprise value, far below the 52.9% historical three-year CAGR [2] and the 42.2% FY2026 consensus growth [3]. If consensus revenue holds for two years, the implied return is 24.2% a year [3]. Consensus is dated after the 10-K, so these figures are forward-looking.

Key risks are credit quality, card-fee regulation and deposit funding, which grew 45.3% and supports the balance sheet [1]. The Piotroski score of 4 of 7 adds a caution on quality [2].
key_takeaways: Operating leverage should keep earnings compounding: operating expenses fell to 17.5% of revenue from 21.3%, lifting diluted EPS 44.9% [1].
Credit costs are the swing factor: gross margin fell to 42.0% from 45.6% as expected credit loss rose 32.7%, so provisioning discipline decides margins [1].
Valuation looks undemanding on a reverse DCF: the current enterprise value implies only 4.0% annual revenue growth, versus 42.2% FY2026 consensus growth [2][3].
Funding is the watch item: deposits grew 45.3% and borrowings rose to US$4.4 billion, while latest TTM free cash flow turned negative [1][2].
business_overview:
Nu Holdings, founded in 2013 and incorporated in the Cayman Islands, provides credit and prepaid cards, deposit accounts, personal and secured loans, investments, insurance and mobile services through one app [1]. Its products span Brazil, Mexico, Colombia and, prospectively, the United States, and it had 131.0 million customers at year-end 2025 [1]. Deposits reached US$41.9 billion, up 45.3% in dollars, and total assets rose 50% to US$74.9 billion [1]. The model is a single consolidated group rather than separately reported segments, so business lines are assessed through revenue and funding lines [1].

Credit remains the core revenue engine. Loan interest income rose 57.4% to US$4,784.3 million, the largest dollar increase of any interest line, and loans to customers reached US$9.4 billion from US$5.3 billion [1]. Credit card interest rose 20.9% to US$4,597.8 million, the slowest growing of the large interest lines, while the card receivables balance grew to US$21.7 billion from US$14.6 billion [1]. Deposit-funded assets grew fastest, with interest income on amortized-cost assets up 78.6% to US$2,284.6 million, but interest expense on deposits rose 65.5% to US$3,876.5 million, which is the main pressure on the spread [1].

Recent initiatives include more than 100 product launches in 2025, among them Brazilian payroll loans and a Colombian subscription card, and the acquisition of Hyperplane in July 2024 [1]. Consensus, dated after the 10-K, expects FY2027 EPS of US$1.06 with a wide range of US$0.78 to US$1.23 [3]. Consolidated net income of US$2,871.7 million is the most reliable measure of the 2025 result [1][2].
market_position:
Nu operates a digital financial services platform in Brazil, Mexico and Colombia, where the five largest incumbents hold 68% to 80% of loans and deposits [1]. The company estimates the retail financial revenue pool in these markets at US$227.9 billion in 2025 and holds a share of about 5% [1]. Within Brazil's card market, Nu held 14.7% of total credit card purchase volume in 2025, up from 14.2% in 2024 and 8.7% in 2021 (ABECS data) [1]. Purchase volume reached US$141.7 billion, up 13% in reported dollars and 17% FX-neutral [1].

Scale is the clearest sign of position. Customers reached 131.0 million at year-end 2025, up 15.0%, including 113 million in Brazil, 14.1 million in Mexico and over 4 million in Colombia [1]. Digital banks held over 8% of Brazilian individual loans by September 2025, up from below 1% in 2018 [1]. Customer acquisition is largely organic, with 80% to 90% of new customers acquired without paid channels each year, and customer acquisition cost was US$7.4 with paid marketing about 32% of it [1]. Monthly ARPAC rose to US$13.3 from US$11.3, and net churn averaged 0.1% per month [1]. The 20-F does not disclose customer concentration or any major customer, consistent with a retail base [1].

Market position is weaker in the newer markets. Colombian deposits reached US$2.5 billion after the Cuenta Nu launch in mid-2024, and Mexico's GDP growth slowed to 0.6% in 2025 from 1.5% [1]. The U.S. bank, Nubank N.A., received conditional OCC approval on January 29, 2026, but has not started banking operations and still needs FDIC and Federal Reserve approvals, so it contributed no reported performance in 2025 [1]. Consensus is dated after the 10-K and its FY2026 EV/Sales of 2.2x and forward P/E of 14.5x at US$12.36 per share suggest the market is pricing the core Brazilian franchise rather than the international build-out [3].
operating_results:
Nu Holdings reported 2025 revenue of US$15,774.8 million, up 37.0%, with interest income supplying 85.2% of the total [1]. Net income rose 45.6% to US$2,871.7 million and diluted EPS rose 44.9% to US$0.5846, while diluted share count grew only 0.4% [1]. Operating leverage was the main driver of profit growth. Operating expenses rose 12.0% to US$2,752.9 million, falling to 17.5% of revenue from 21.3% [1].

The gross margin, however, compressed. Costs of financial and transactional services rose 46.1%, faster than revenue, led by deposit interest expense (+65.5%) and expected credit loss (+32.7%), so gross margin fell to 42.0% from 45.6% [1]. Expected credit loss on cards and loans held at 15.4% of receivables in both years, so the increase reflects portfolio growth rather than a deterioration in the ratio [1]. Credit and prepaid card income rose 24.6% to US$1,720.3 million, while late fees rose 33.9% to US$385.0 million [1]. Net income grew faster than revenue, helped by a lower effective tax rate of 25.8% against 29.4%, which management attributed to recognized deferred tax assets [1].

Cash generation strengthened alongside earnings. Operating cash flow reached US$3,500.5 million against US$2,399.1 million in 2024, and capital expenditure of US$340.8 million left illustrative free cash flow of US$3,159.7 million [1]. Working capital absorbed US$11,078.7 million, mainly from a US$12,445.8 million rise in card and loan receivables, and financing supplied about 42% of the US$5,448.4 million increase in cash [1]. The company paid no dividends or buybacks. Reported growth also benefits from currency effects: deposits grew 45.3% in US dollars but 29.0% on an FX-neutral basis [1]. Consensus, dated after the 10-K, expects FY2026 revenue of US$22,438.6 million (+42.2%) and EPS of US$0.85 [3].
risk_assessment:
The largest risk is credit quality. Nu states that non-performing loans are expected to rise in absolute terms as the book grows, and that it "cannot guarantee" reserves will cover actual losses [1]. Expected credit loss grew 32.7% to US$4,204.9 million, and the ratio held at 15.4% of receivables, so any rise in that ratio would hit earnings directly [1]. Financial and cash assets made up 54.7% of total assets at year-end, carrying investment and derivative losses that the filing calls potentially significant, and Nu chose not to hedge foreign exchange exposure from its Brazilian, Colombian and Mexican investments [1].

Revenue concentration and regulation form the second risk. Card fees and card interest made up 40.0% of 2025 revenue, down from 45.0%, but the mix remains weighted toward cards [1]. Regulation could push customers away from the credit book through the Over-Indebtedness Law and Decree No. 11,567's R$600 minimum threshold, and fee or interest caps would reduce revenue where introduced [1]. Open finance rules also make it easier for customers to move credit to competitors [1]. Consensus, dated after the 10-K, sees FY2027 EPS revisions down 4.6% over the last 90 days, which may reflect part of this risk [3].

The third risk is operational. All transactions run through the mobile app, the filing acknowledges "disruptions, outages and other performance problems," and Nu carries no property or business-interruption insurance [1]. Mastercard authorizes card transactions, and some providers are sole-source [1]. Financial quality scores point the same way: the Piotroski F-score is 4 of 7, with failures on asset turnover and return on assets [2]. The 20-F risk section, as analysed, does not cover all disclosures, so further risks may exist [1].
competitors_analysis:
Among US-listed peers, Inter & Co (INTR) is the closest business-model match, since it is also a Brazilian digital bank, and SoFi (SOFI) is the closest model on app-first lending. PagSeguro (PAGS) is included for its Brazilian payments and card franchise at a comparable scale [2]. Nu's revenue growth has been the fastest in the set over three years, from US$2,971 million in 2022 to US$10,627 million in 2025, but growth has slowed each year, to 89.6%, 46.8% and 28.5% [2]. Note that the peer data use a revenue base of US$10,627 million, which differs from the US$15,774.8 million in the 20-F, so growth and multiples are not directly comparable to the filing [1][2].

On 2025 growth Nu trailed both peers, with SoFi at 38.3% and Inter at 31.3% [2]. Nu's free cash flow rose to US$3,160 million, with FCF conversion near 1 in each year from 2023 to 2025, the most consistent in the set. Inter's free cash flow was larger in absolute terms, at US$7,160 million in 2025, though its conversion ratio is volatile [2]. SoFi's FCF was negative in 2024 and 2025 [2].

Valuation is where Nu stands apart. Its 2025 EV/Sales of 5.86 was second only to SoFi's 8.38, and well above Inter's 2.89 and PagSeguro's 2.73 [2]. Its price-to-book of 7.20 was the highest in the group [2]. Consensus, dated after the 10-K, values Nu at a forward P/E of 14.5x and forward EV/Sales of 2.2x, which signals that the market pricing depends on which year's earnings are used [3]. The peer data do not provide Nu's EBITDA, gross profit or ROIC, so profitability cannot be benchmarked against peers on those measures [2].

investment_theses.thesis: Operating leverage keeps EPS compounding even as gross margin compresses.
investment_theses.evidence: Operating expenses fell to 17.5% of revenue from 21.3%, net income rose 45.6% and diluted EPS rose 44.9% to US$0.5846 [1].
investment_theses.signpost: Operating expenses stay below 20% of revenue in each 2026 quarterly report, and FY2026 diluted EPS lands near the US$0.85 consensus [3].
investment_theses.invalidation: Operating expenses return above 21.3% of revenue, or FY2026 EPS falls below the US$0.80 low end of the consensus range [3].

investment_theses.thesis: Credit losses stay contained at about 15% of receivables, so gross margin stabilises.
investment_theses.evidence: Expected credit loss rose 32.7% to US$4,204.9 million, but the ratio held at 15.4% of receivables in both years, and gross margin fell to 42.0% from 45.6% [1].
investment_theses.signpost: The expected credit loss ratio on cards and loans stays at or below 15.4% in each 2026 quarterly report.
investment_theses.invalidation: The expected credit loss ratio rises above 15.4%, or non-performing loans grow faster than the loan book.

investment_theses.thesis: The current valuation prices in a sharp growth slowdown, so the stock can re-rate if revenue keeps growing.
investment_theses.evidence: The reverse DCF implies 4.0% annual revenue growth at the current enterprise value [2], against a 52.9% historical three-year CAGR [2] and 42.2% FY2026 consensus growth [3]. EV/Sales of 5.86 in 2025 was about twice the peers' 2.7 to 2.9 [2].
investment_theses.signpost: FY2026 revenue reported in the 2026 20-F (early 2027) at or above the US$22.3 billion low end of consensus [3].
investment_theses.invalidation: FY2026 revenue falls below US$22.3 billion, or FY2027 consensus EPS is cut further from the current US$1.06 (already down 4.6% over 90 days) [3].

investment_theses.thesis: Deposit funding keeps the balance sheet self-sustaining without new equity.
investment_theses.evidence: Deposits reached US$41.9 billion, up 45.3%, and borrowings rose to US$4.4 billion from US$1.7 billion [1]. Net cash was US$19.0 billion at year-end 2025 [2], but TTM free cash flow to the latest quarter was -US$625.9 million [2].
investment_theses.signpost: Deposit growth stays above 25% on an FX-neutral basis, and TTM free cash flow turns positive in the FY2026 20-F (early 2027).
investment_theses.invalidation: Deposit growth falls below 20% (FX-neutral), or borrowings grow faster than deposits for a full year.
